extracted.intended_audience: NLP researchers and practitioners working on patent analysis and patent-text generation
extracted.subtask_description: A broad survey of natural language processing (NLP) methods, datasets, tasks, and evaluation metrics specific to patent documents, aimed at helping researchers develop and evaluate models for patent analysis and generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patentable a technical solution must be (1) new, (2) involve an inventive step (non-obviousness), and (3) be industrially applicable / have utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the substantive criteria examiners apply during examination and as a core concept for tasks like novelty prediction; note that utility requirements may be applied less strictly by some offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent document element requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent documents normally include publication information, title, bibliometric information (applicants, inventors, assignees, examiners, attorneys), patent classification codes, citations, abstract, drawings, background, detailed description, and claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sections are canonical inputs/targets for many patent NLP tasks — e.g., use claims for scope, description for long-context analysis, drawings when relevant; treat each element according to its typical function in patent processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims formal/structural requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim is a single sentence which describes the invention in specific features that make the invention novel and not obvious; claims define the legal scope of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims require extreme precision and consistent terminology; generation tasks must respect single-sentence structure and legal scope semantics to be defensible and useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments / no-new-matter rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments must not introduce novel features (inventive content); introducing new matter can cause loss of original priority date or rejection/challenge of the file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting or generating amended text, do not add content that extends the original disclosure; in workflow/data curation, flag additions that could be new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication timing / public access
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent documents are typically publicly accessible about 18 months after the application or first filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This affects dataset availability and reproducibility; researchers should account for publication timing when building or using corpora.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and consistency requirement of patent language
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent language has higher precision and information density than everyday text; terminology must be used consistently and sentences often include many qualifiers to delimit scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models and evaluation should prioritize precise, legally-relevant wording over readability; generation anti-patterns include small lexical deviations that change legal meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long context characteristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent descriptions are very long (average patent description tokens can exceed 11,000), much longer than typical LLM context windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design models or preprocessing to cope with long contexts (long-context LLMs, chunking, retrieval-augmented methods); avoid evaluating only on titles/abstracts since they are highly generic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical language and self-defined terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents regularly define specialized or newly coined terms that may deviate from normal usage and may not appear in general corpora.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embeddings and LLMs trained on general text may not capture such terms; domain adaptation, fine-tuning, or explicit term handling is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM domain suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Although LLMs are promising for patent tasks, their effectiveness depends on domain-specific training; many existing LLMs tested in the patent domain have been relatively small (e.g., GPT-2 scale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should evaluate LLMs carefully in the patent domain and consider fine-tuning on patent corpora, long-context models, and curated datasets to address domain mismatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset curation and gold vs silver standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Gold standard datasets for generation tasks are human-written; for tasks like patent simplification, only silver-standard (automatically generated) datasets may exist due to high cost of expert annotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about dataset provenance; treat silver-standard outputs as noisy labels and validate with human evaluation where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification scheme hierarchy (IPC/CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification schemes such as IPC and CPC are hierarchical (sections, classes, sub-classes, main groups, sub-groups) and are commonly used labels for subject classification tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model outputs and evaluation should account for hierarchy (e.g., partial matches at different levels); use appropriate label granularity for the task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject classification evaluation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Three evaluation methods: top prediction (top-1 matches main class), top N guesses (one of top-n matches main class), and all-categories method (top-1 included in main + incidental classes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the evaluation method that matches application needs — top-N is more flexible; all-categories is stricter for multi-label correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification metrics and aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Common metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1; aggregation across classes via macro-averaging (equal weight per class) or micro-averaging (aggregate counts — better for class imbalance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both macro and micro where relevant; justify averaging choice based on class imbalance and task goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information retrieval metrics for patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard IR metrics: precision, recall, mean average precision (MAP); patent-specific metric: PRES (patent retrieval evaluation score) which measures deviation of actual ranks from ideal ranking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use PRES for patent retrieval benchmarking when appropriate; clearly define relevance and retrieval cutoffs; MAP and precision/recall remain standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text generation evaluation (human and automated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human evaluation (accuracy, fluency, coherence, relevance) is gold standard; automated metrics include BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, BERTScore; a keystroke-based evaluation measures saved keystrokes for autoregressive completion (proposed for claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use automated metrics for fast comparisons but complement with human evaluation for legal/precision-sensitive outputs; keystroke metrics are useful for productivity-focused evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent lifecycle constraints relevant to NLP tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent lifecycle splits pre-grant and post-grant stages; pre-grant involves drafting, search, examination (formal/legal/technical compliance), amendments; post-grant involves publication, maintenance fees, enforcement, validity challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different NLP tasks map to lifecycle stages (e.g., novelty prediction pre-grant, litigation prediction post-grant); consider stage-specific metadata and constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings / figures conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings contain reference numbers that must be named consistently; patent figures are not supposed to contain significant text beyond reference numbers; figures vary in resolution and informativeness (often generic sketches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat drawings as auxiliary and noisy visual data; when using image-based models, expect variable quality and that image-only classification performs worse than text or multimodal methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metadata as signals (benefits and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metadata (citations, classification codes, inventors, applicants, assignees, examiners) can improve retrieval/classification performance but typically lack details about the invention's technical nuances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine metadata with textual information for improved representations; be cautious about over-reliance on coarse metadata for technical understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid / multimodal analysis recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hybrid methods that leverage text, images (drawings), and classification codes tend to be promising because single-source methods (text-only, image-only, metadata-only) have limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design multimodal pipelines where appropriate; weigh extra complexity against gains in specific tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of shared tasks and benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Shared tasks and workshops (CLEF-IP, NTCIR, TREC-CHEM) provide curated datasets and standard tasks enabling fair comparisons and progress in patent retrieval, classification, translation, and other tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use shared task datasets for benchmarking; follow shared-task evaluation protocols to enable comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization cautions for novelty labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Proxy labels for novelty (e.g., patents connected to awards or cross-office rejections) may deviate from formal novelty definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building novelty prediction datasets, carefully justify proxies and be aware of potential misalignment with legal novelty concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image-specific limitations and approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Image-based patent classification/retrieval is challenging due to generic diagrams, CAD complexity, and low resolution; CNNs and transformer-based metric-learning have been applied but perform worse than text-based methods alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use images as supplementary signals; prefer hybrid approaches; invest in domain-specific image preprocessing and model design if relying on figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figure caption generation behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent figure captions are often boilerplate and minimal (e.g., 'Figure n depicts another embodiment of the invention') to satisfy formal requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect limited semantic content in many captions; when evaluating caption generation, account for high prevalence of templated captions and consider richer contextual grounding (description text) for meaningful captions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of data availability & access issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Although many patent offices publish raw documents and sometimes bulk downloads, curated task-specific datasets are scarcer, and data access may be limited by paid services or practical hurdles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document dataset collection choices and licensing; prefer public datasets (e.g., HUPD, BigPatent) when possible and be explicit about coverage and preprocessing.
